newsitem.title: USA: Magellan's Stansky taking time to rejig fund.
newsitem.headline: Magellan's Stansky taking time to rejig fund.

text.p: Fidelity Investments Magellan Fund manager Bob Stansky cut his investments in bonds during July, but has reshaped the massive mutual fund at a much slower pace than many analysts expected.
"He's going a lot slower than I expected him to," said David O'Leary, president of Alpha Equity Research of Portsmouth, N.H.
Many analysts said when Stansky took the helm in June from former manager Jeffrey Vinik that he would quickly slash Magellan's massive holdings in bonds.

However, at the end of July, the most recent month data is available, assets invested in bonds stood at 15.6 percent, down from 18.1 percent at the end of June and 19.3 percent at the end of May. U.S. bonds and notes remained in the top three positions of Magellan's top 10 largest holdings.

At the beginning of August, Fidelity said on its Internet site (http://www.fid-inv.com) that Stansky was "proceeding deliberately" in reviewing the fund and the second quarter earnings season would be important for determing Magellan's direction.
Stansky was not available to comment on Thursday.
O'Leary said Stansky may be averaging out of bonds by selling $50 to $100 million or so a day of the more than $8 billion invested in U.S. treasuries.
"Vinik got it wrong by buying them and, if (Stansky) blew them out all at once, and rates topped and started to decline, Magellan shareholders would lose twice," he said.
Phil Orlando, chief investment officer of Value Line Asset Management, said Stansky may be holding bonds while waiting for stock prices to become more attractive.

"If this were November or December of any year, I think he would have gone hog wild to equities right away," Orlando said. "In terms of seasonality, September and October tend to be the months of the year in which the market tends to have its weakest price performance."

Both Orlando and O'Leary said they still expected Stansky to sell off the entire bond stake in favor of traditional growth stocks. O'Leary said Stansky will reshape the fund to look like his former Fidelity Growth Company Fund, with a high proportion of holdings in technology, finance, retail and healthcare shares.
However, at the end of July, Stansky had moved slowly in that direction.
Assets in technology stocks rose to 5.5 percent at the end of July from 3.7 percent at the end of June and 2.6 percent at the end of May, according to Fidelity's Internet site.

Financial stocks rose to 7.0 percent from 6.6 percent in June and 5.8 percent at the end of May, while retail stocks remained flat at 4.8 percent at the end of July versus June and rose from 3.6 percent at the end of May.
Stansky still had a negligible portion of assets invested in healthcare companies at the end of July.
"It looks like the Fidelity managers as a whole look like they're betting on a slowdown," O'Leary said. "They have very defensive positions."
